title: Task Scheduler
description:
# Task Scheduler

Given an array `tasks`, where each uppercase letter represents one CPU task type, and a non-negative cooldown `n`, return the minimum number of time units needed to execute every task.

Each task takes exactly one unit of time. The CPU may execute one task or stay idle during each unit. Two executions of the same task type must have at least `n` full time units between them. Different task types do not block each other.

## Example

Input: `tasks = ["A","A","A","B","B","B"], n = 2`

Output: `8`

One optimal schedule is `A, B, idle, A, B, idle, A, B`.

## Constraints

`1 <= tasks.length <= 10^4`. Every task is an uppercase English letter. `0 <= n <= 100`.
initialCode: class Solution { public int leastInterval(char[] tasks, int n) { return 0; } }

solutions.name: Frequency Frame Formula
solutions.description:
## Approach

Count each task type. Let `maxFrequency` be the largest count, and let `maxCount` be how many task types have that count. The most frequent tasks form `maxFrequency - 1` frames of length `n + 1`, plus the final group of tied most-frequent tasks.

## Key Insight

Only the most frequent task types can force idle time. If all other tasks fill the frame gaps, the answer is just `tasks.length`; otherwise the frame formula gives the required length.

## Complexity Analysis

Counting and scanning the 26 letters costs `O(m + 26)`, where `m` is `tasks.length`. The frequency array uses `O(1)` space.

solutions.name: Max Heap Cycle Simulation
solutions.description:
## Approach

Put remaining task frequencies into a max heap. Each scheduling round can execute at most `n + 1` distinct task types. Remove up to that many largest counts, decrement them, then push unfinished tasks back for the next round.

## Key Insight

A full round consumes one cooldown window. If work remains after the round, the round must count as `n + 1` time units; if no work remains, only the tasks actually executed in the last round count.

## Complexity Analysis

Let `T` be the final schedule length. Every simulated execution touches a heap of at most 26 letters, so the time complexity is `O(T log 26)`, effectively linear for a fixed alphabet. Space is `O(1)`.

solutions.name: Time Simulation with Cooldown Queue
solutions.description:
## Approach

Simulate one time unit at a time. A max heap stores task types that are currently available, and a FIFO cooldown queue stores pairs of ready time and remaining count. At every time unit, move ready tasks back to the heap, execute one available task if possible, and queue it again if work remains.

## Key Insight

This route models the rule literally: a task executed at time `t` may next run at `t + n + 1`. It is slower than the formula but is the easiest way to debug off-by-one cooldown mistakes.

## Complexity Analysis

The simulation runs for `T` time units and heap operations use at most 26 letters, so the time complexity is `O(T log 26)`. The heap and queue store `O(26)` task types.

solutions.name: Sorted Counts Round Simulation
solutions.description:
## Approach

Keep the 26 frequencies sorted. In each round, take from the largest counts for up to `n + 1` slots, decrementing those counts. Sort again before the next round. Stop early inside the last round as soon as no task remains.

## Key Insight

This is a heap-free simulation of the same cooldown window idea. Re-sorting a fixed-size frequency array is simple and still constant-factor bounded because there are only 26 task types.

## Complexity Analysis

The simulation may consider `T` schedule slots, and each round sorts 26 counters, so the time complexity is `O(T * 26 log 26)`. The counter array is fixed size, so space is `O(1)`.
